summary: This RFC suggests a simple way for a workstation to fetch mail from a mailbox server, with sending done through SMTP. It is the first version of the Post Office Protocol and was replaced by RFC 937.

plainLanguage.summary: Your mail waits at the post office, and you walk over with your computer to pick it up. This describes how to ask for it.

how does pop fetch mail from a server

subtitle: Simple protocol for workstations to fetch mail from a server

tldr.problem: Workstations need a simple way to retrieve their mail from a central mail server without implementing complex mail protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 918 defines a simple text command protocol on TCP where a client authenticates with USER and PASS commands, then retrieves all mail from a named mailbox with RETR or RDEL, optionally with automatic deletion.
tldr.outcome: This was the first version of POP, later improved by RFC 937 (POP2) and subsequent versions.

facts.label: Commands
facts.value: 8: USER, PASS, RETR, RDEL, RCEV, RCVD, QUIT, NOOP, RSET

facts.label: Response codes
facts.value: +OK for success, -ERR for error, #xxx for byte count

today: RFC 918 was the first version of POP, replaced by RFC 937 (POP2) and subsequently by RFC 1081 (POP3). Modern email systems primarily use POP3 or IMAP.

sections.title: Purpose and Design
sections.content:
RFC 918 specifies the Post Office Protocol (POP), a simple method for workstations to dynamically access mail from a mailbox server. POP is intended as a companion to SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol): SMTP sends mail from a workstation to the mail server, while POP retrieves mail from the server back to the workstation.

The protocol is transaction-based: the client authenticates with username and password, selects a mailbox for reading with either RETR (read without deleting) or RDEL (read and delete), requests the mail data, and ends the session. The server locks the mailbox during the transaction to prevent concurrent access.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is simple: connect, log in, pick a mailbox, download all the mail, and disconnect. The mail can stay on the server or be deleted.

sections.title: Commands and Protocol Flow
sections.content:
The client opens a TCP connection and waits for the server's greeting message. It then authenticates using USER <name> followed by PASS <password>, with the server responding +OK or -ERR to each. The client requests mail retrieval with either RETR <mailbox> (read without deleting) or RDEL <mailbox> (read and delete), and the server responds with #xxx showing the character count.

The client sends RCEV to request transmission of the mail data, the server sends the mail contents, and the client sends RCVD to confirm receipt. For RDEL transactions, RCVD triggers the actual deletion. The client may also send NOOP (no operation) or RSET (reset transaction), and ends with QUIT to close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands are: USER and PASS to log in, RETR or RDEL to select a mailbox, RCEV to ask for the mail, RCVD to confirm you got it, and QUIT to disconnect.

sections.title: Simplicity and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 918 emphasizes simplicity: the protocol uses plain text commands, takes only a few commands to complete a transaction, and requires minimal parsing. The server is stateless between transactions. All mail in a selected mailbox must be retrieved together; there is no way to request individual messages or to examine a message list first.

The mailbox is locked during the transaction to prevent the mail server and client from interfering with each other. However, there is no mechanism to selectively retrieve messages, flag them for deletion, or maintain state between sessions. These limitations motivated improvements in later versions of the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is simple but limited: you get everything from a mailbox at once. You cannot pick specific messages or leave mail partially read.
